The central question is: when you combine sliding window attention layers (which only attend to a local neighborhood of tokens) with full attention layers (which attend to the entire context), how should you decide which cached key-value pairs to evict under memory pressure — and does the right answer change when you're running the model on sequences longer than it was trained on?

The key concepts are: KV cache eviction (dropping stored key-value pairs to save memory, typically by some scoring heuristic like attention mass or recency), sliding window attention (each token attends only to the last w tokens, so distant KV pairs are structurally invisible anyway), full attention layers (every token is a potential attendee, making eviction decisions genuinely lossy), and context length generalization (running inference at sequence lengths outside the training distribution, where positional encodings and learned attention patterns may degrade).

What a beginner misses is that eviction policy correctness is not uniform across layer types: in sliding window layers, evicting tokens outside the window is free by construction, whereas in full attention layers the same eviction is a real information loss — and crucially, the full attention layers are precisely where the model concentrates its long-range retrieval, so bad eviction there compounds disproportionately. The expert further worries that context length generalization breaks the implicit assumptions baked into eviction scoring heuristics: attention scores used to rank "importance" were calibrated on in-distribution sequence lengths, and at extrapolated lengths those scores can become miscalibrated — tokens that appear low-salience under the distorted attention distribution may actually carry critical information. The deepest concern is that hybrid architectures create a false sense of safety: sliding window layers look cheap to manage, which tempts engineers to apply aggressive eviction budgets globally, inadvertently starving the full attention layers of the headroom they need precisely when sequences are long enough to require genuine long-range recall.

The core failure mode is attention score miscalibration under distribution shift: models trained at sequence length L learn softmax temperature and score magnitude implicitly calibrated to that length, and when you run inference at 4L or 8L, the raw dot-product logits before softmax are computed over a population of keys the model never saw during training, causing the softmax to either over-concentrate (one or two tokens absorb nearly all mass) or flatten (scores become near-uniform noise) depending on architecture details. This matters for eviction because heuristics like H2O's heavy-hitter scoring or SnapKV's pooled attention ranking treat high attention mass as a proxy for semantic importance — but if the distribution is pathologically peaked due to extrapolation artifacts, you'll over-retain a small set of "attention sink" tokens (often the BOS token and early punctuation, as documented in StreamingLLM by Xiao et al. 2023) while evicting genuinely informative mid-sequence tokens that received suppressed scores purely due to positional interference. The positional encoding choice sharply modulates this failure: learned absolute encodings (GPT-2/3 style) collapse almost immediately past the training length because out-of-vocabulary position embeddings produce near-random key/query projections, making attention scores in those layers essentially meaningless for eviction ranking. RoPE (used in LLaMA, Mistral) degrades more gracefully because relative position is encoded in the rotation, but at extrapolated lengths the rotation angles enter a frequency regime never seen in training — YaRN and LongRoPE both show that without explicit frequency rescaling, RoPE models exhibit a "lost in the middle" pattern where mid-sequence tokens receive systematically lower attention than positionally proximal ones, biasing eviction toward dropping exactly the tokens that carry long-range content. ALiBi (used in MPT, BLOOM) is the most eviction-friendly at extrapolation because its linear distance penalty is length-agnostic by construction — scores degrade smoothly with distance rather than catastrophically, so the rank-ordering of token importance, while imperfect, remains more trustworthy as a basis for eviction decisions than the distorted landscapes RoPE or learned absolute produce at out-of-distribution lengths.

The pyramid assumption breaks, and it breaks specifically because the hybrid interleaving pattern creates a non-monotonic information flow that the pyramid's depth-as-proxy-for-abstraction logic cannot capture. PyramidKV's rationale is that lower layers need larger budgets because they carry raw token-level information that higher layers compress into abstractions — but in a hybrid architecture like Gemma 2 (which alternates local/global attention every other layer) or Mistral's sliding window design, a full attention layer at depth 8 sitting between sliding window layers at depths 7 and 9 is not doing the same job as a full attention layer at depth 2; it is performing long-range retrieval after the sliding window layers have already filtered and transformed the representation, making it functionally more like a retrieval bottleneck than an early feature extractor. Empirical attention entropy analysis on models like Gemma 2 9B shows that full attention layers at mid and late depths exhibit higher attention spread across the sequence than early layers, which is the opposite of what the pyramid predicts — these layers are actively pulling from distant positions, not compressing local context. The correct abstraction is not a pyramid but a layer-type-conditional budget: sliding window layers get minimal budgets (only the local window, structurally), and full attention layers get budgets sized by their measured retrieval demand regardless of depth, which likely means flat or even inverse allocation relative to PyramidKV's scheme for the full-attention subset. Mistral's and Google's inference engineering teams have not published explicit eviction budget schedules for their hybrid models, but the practical implication is that any system naively porting PyramidKV onto a Gemma 2 or Mixtral-style architecture will under-protect exactly the mid-to-late full attention layers that are doing the heaviest long-range lifting, producing retrieval failures that look like context length bugs but are actually eviction policy mismatches.

The practical implementation of dynamic eviction is to compute a cheap proxy for retrieval demand — typically attention entropy or the Gini coefficient of the attention distribution — during the prefill pass, then set per-layer budgets before the decode phase begins; this is essentially what AdaKV (Zhang et al., 2024) does, allocating budget across heads and layers proportional to measured attention concentration during prefill. The inference cost of this approach has two components: the measurement overhead (computing entropy or Gini across all heads during prefill adds roughly 3–8% latency on top of the attention computation itself, which is acceptable) and the scheduling overhead (deciding budgets and reorganizing the KV cache layout adds memory management complexity that can cause fragmentation in systems like vLLM's paged attention, which assumes relatively static block allocation). The deeper problem is that prefill-time demand measurement may not predict decode-time demand accurately for long generative sequences — a document that looks low-retrieval during prefill may require heavy cross-attention during generation when the model starts synthesizing across sources, meaning you've already committed to a budget that's too small. The most honest current answer is that production systems like those running LLaMA 3 70B at 128K context are using coarse static-dynamic hybrids: statically protect full attention layers more than sliding window layers, dynamically adjust within a pre-specified range based on sequence length bins, and accept that the policy is a heuristic approximation rather than an optimal solution — the compute cost of true per-request optimality is not yet justified by the quality delta on most deployment workloads.

The most principled training-time intervention is eviction-aware training: exposing the model during training to the same KV-dropping operations it will face at inference time, so that attention patterns are learned under the constraint that some keys will be unavailable, forcing the model to concentrate retrieval signals in ways that survive eviction. This is the core idea behind ScissorHands and, more explicitly, GEAR and CLA (Cross-Layer Attention) — in CLA, certain layers are trained to share KV caches across adjacent layers, which has the side effect of forcing the model to learn attention distributions that are robust to cache reuse and implicitly more concentrated and trustworthy as importance signals. A cleaner direct approach is attention regularization during training: adding an auxiliary loss that penalizes diffuse, low-entropy attention distributions in full attention layers, pushing the model toward sparser, more interpretable attention that makes high-mass tokens genuinely semantically important rather than artifacts of softmax normalization — Anthropic's work on attention head superposition and DeepMind's work on attention sharpening in Gemma suggest this direction is viable but has not been explicitly tied to eviction proxy quality. The training-time intervention with the most direct empirical validation is landmark attention (Mohtashami & Jaggi, 2023), which inserts special landmark tokens into training sequences and teaches the model to route long-range retrieval through them — these landmarks then serve as natural eviction boundaries at inference time, making the proxy problem tractable because you evict non-landmark spans rather than individual tokens whose importance is ambiguous. The fundamental reason all these interventions help is the same: default transformer training has no gradient signal that rewards making attention scores interpretable as importance proxies — the model only needs scores to produce correct outputs, not to be honest about token salience — so without explicit training pressure, the correlation between attention mass and eviction-worthiness is incidental and breaks under distribution shift.

Yes, and this is an underappreciated tension: diffuse attention patterns are not merely noise — they are one mechanism by which transformers implement implicit averaging and smoothing operations that contribute to representation quality, and forcing sparsity via regularization or landmark routing compresses that capacity into fewer pathways through the residual stream. Anthropic's interpretability work on attention head function categorization found that a non-trivial fraction of heads in large models perform "induction" and "fuzzy matching" operations that depend on attending broadly across many tokens with low but distributed mass — these heads would be systematically damaged by entropy-minimizing regularization because their function is diffuse attention. The landmark token case is subtler but potentially more damaging: by funneling long-range information through discrete bottleneck tokens, you are implicitly imposing a lossy compression at the landmark boundaries, and the residual stream at non-landmark positions loses the direct gradient path to distant context — empirically, Mohtashami & Jaggi noted that landmark attention models showed degraded performance on tasks requiring fine-grained cross-sentence coreference compared to full attention baselines, which is precisely the signature of bottleneck compression destroying the distributed representations that coreference resolution requires. The residual stream impact is concrete: in standard transformers, information from distant tokens reaches later layers via two paths — direct attention (which eviction targets) and accumulated residual contributions from earlier layers (which eviction does not touch) — and diffuse attention patterns are part of how the model balances these two paths; sparsifying attention shifts more burden onto the residual accumulation path, which may not have the capacity to compensate, particularly in smaller models where residual rank is already a bottleneck. The honest synthesis is that eviction-proxy reliability and representational completeness are in genuine tension, not merely an engineering tradeoff: the same diffuseness that makes attention scores unreliable as importance proxies may be load-bearing for model quality, meaning the optimal training-time intervention is not maximum sparsity but rather structured sparsity that preserves averaging heads while concentrating retrieval heads — a decomposition that current training recipes do not explicitly enforce and that would require head-type-aware regularization to achieve safely.
